sections.title: The Parameters of the Mitzva
sections.html:
One who finds a bird's nest and wishes to take the mother that is sitting on the chicks or the eggs in order to eat her meat may not do so, for the Torah commanded not to exploit the mother's responsibility to guard her chicks or eggs in order to catch her. Rather, he should first chase the mother away from the nest until she flies off and does not try to return to it, and only afterwards may he try to catch her like any other bird. Likewise, it is forbidden to take the chicks or the eggs while the mother is sitting on them; rather, only after he has chased the mother away so that he cannot catch her may he take the chicks or the eggs. As it is stated (Devarim 22:6-7): "If a bird's nest chances before you on the way, in any tree or on the ground, with chicks or eggs, and the mother sitting upon the chicks or upon the eggs – you shall not take the mother together with the young. You shall surely send away the mother, and the young you may take for yourself, so that it may be well with you and you may prolong your days."

The mitzva applies to species of birds that are kosher for eating, which people are accustomed to take for food. But with a non-kosher bird, it is permitted to take the mother together with the eggs and the chicks (SA YD 292:1).

The mitzva applies only to wild birds that do not belong to a person, as it is stated: "If a bird's nest chances before you" – in ownerless places. But in a nest that is in a person's possession there is no prohibition, because the mother, the eggs and the chicks belong to him, and therefore he may take them whenever he wishes (Mishna Ḥullin 138b). Therefore, although a hen is also a bird, one who raises hens may take a hen off her eggs, and take eggs and chicks from under a hen that is brooding on them. The same law applies to pigeons in a person's possession: he may take from them without restriction.1

If he sinned and took the mother while she was sitting or hovering over the chicks or the eggs, he should set her free, and thereby he rectifies his sin. But if he slaughtered her, although her meat is permitted to eat, he is liable to lashes, since he can no longer rectify his sin. Likewise, if she died on her own, since he can no longer send her away and rectify his sin, he is liable to lashes (Ḥullin 141a; SA YD 292:6).2

sections.title: The Reasons for the Mitzva
sections.html:
One of the beloved and profound areas of Torah study is 'the reasons for the mitzvot.' Its importance is twofold: because of its value as study, and because understanding them creates identification with the mitzva and a desire to fulfill it. However, it must be emphasized that we are not capable of understanding the absolute reason for the establishment of a mitzva, because the human intellect is limited and is unable to understand the thoughts of the Creator and the depth of the Torah's intent. Therefore the reasons are understandings that we grasp in the mitzva, but we do not claim that they are the only reason for the mitzva, and therefore we also do not draw halakhic conclusions from them.

Moreover, in a certain respect it is preferable to fulfill the mitzvot because the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us to fulfill them, and not because we understand their reasons. For this is the virtue of the complete believer: he fulfills the commandments of his Creator even though he does not understand their reason. This is the great praise of Israel, who said "We will do and we will hear" (Shemot 24:7); that is, out of their great devotion to God, they agreed in advance to fulfill everything He would command without any reason other than that this is His will. After this understanding, we may delve into the Torah and the reasons for the mitzvot, and add meaning and joy when fulfilling them.

Three main reasons have been given for the mitzva of shilu'aḥ ha-ken:

The first is to instill in our hearts respect for the value of preserving living creatures. For the most important foundation for the survival of animal species is their ability to raise the next generation, and for this purpose the bird was created with the trait of devoted care for her eggs and fledglings. The prohibition against taking the mother and harming her ability to continue to produce offspring is similar to the prohibition against uprooting a fruit tree, since many fruits grow from it (above 13:1-3). It is permitted to pick the fruit of the tree, for this does not harm the tree, which is the source of life. Likewise, it is permitted to take the chicks and the eggs, provided that one first sends away the mother, who is the source of life for further offspring. The prohibition applies to kosher birds that live in the wild, for regarding birds that are raised in our possession there is no concern, since we will in any case see to it that they continue to multiply. Likewise, regarding non-kosher birds there is no concern, since in any case we will not make an effort to catch many of them, as they are forbidden to us for eating (based on Rabbeinu Baḥya and Sforno, Devarim 22:6).

The second is to strengthen in our hearts the trait of compassion, so that we do not take the mother off her fledglings, but rather first set her free, and only after she has moved away from the nest do we take her fledglings. In the trait that God implanted in the bird, which guards and nurtures her eggs and fledglings, there is an expression of concern and devotion to raising the next generations, to the point that she is ready to risk her life for the sake of her offspring, and it is not proper that we exploit this noble trait of the mother in order to catch her and eat her meat (Ramban, Devarim 22:6; Ḥinukh 545).

According to these reasons, one can understand the reward that the Torah promised to one who sends away the mother, as it is stated, "so that it may be well with you and you may prolong your days": whoever cleaves to the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He, and has compassion on living creatures, will merit that God will have compassion on him, prolong his days and do good to him. The Sages further said that in the merit of this mitzva, childless people merit to be remembered (with offspring), for just as they respected the mother's concern for her fledglings, so they will merit to raise children (Devarim Rabba 6:6).

Another reason is mentioned in the words of the Kabbalists, and it relates to our national situation: when a Jew sends the mother away from her young, and she grieves over her fledglings and flutters her wings, the remembrance of Israel rises before their Father in Heaven, for since the Shekhina went into exile and the Temple was destroyed, the children are in distress and captivity, like orphans and forsaken ones. That is, the mitzva of shilu'aḥ ha-ken relates to a complex and complicated reality: on the one hand, man needs to eat and wants the meat of the bird, the fledglings and the eggs, and on the other hand, it is proper to have pity on the mother caring for her young. And since it is not possible to satisfy all the desires, a person could despair of trying to conduct his life according to ideals. But the Torah guides us to act in the best way possible in our complicated situation: to send away the mother and take the young. And since even within the complicated reality of this world and of the exile, the Children of Israel strive to direct their path according to the values of Torah and morality, compassion is aroused for them, to redeem them from the sufferings and complications of the exile to the Land of Israel and the building of the Temple, so that they will be able to realize all the ideals, and every single creature will be able to live in the way that is perfect for it, and the whole world will be filled with consolation and joy.3

sections.title: Is There a Mitzva to Send Away the Mother Even When the Eggs Are Not Needed?
sections.html:
The Sages said that there is no mitzva to search for a bird's nest in order to fulfill the mitzva, as it is stated: "If a bird's nest chances before you" (Ḥullin 139b). However, a question arose regarding one who is not interested in the fledglings or the eggs and happens upon a bird's nest: is there a mitzva for him to send away the mother and take the fledglings or the eggs?

According to many poskim, only one who needs the fledglings or the eggs has a mitzva to send away the mother in order to take them. But if he does not need them, there is no mitzva for him to send away the mother and take the fledglings. And since this is so, it is not proper to do so, so as not to cause suffering to animals and not to destroy fledglings and eggs for nothing.

However, some say that whoever encounters a bird's nest on his way has a mitzva to send away the mother and take the young. And some Kabbalists hold that it is even proper for every Jew to search for a bird's nest, in order to fulfill the mitzva of shilu'aḥ ha-ken at least once in his life. And there is no prohibition of destruction or of 'tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim' in this, since it is done for the sake of fulfilling the mitzva.

In practice, it seems that the main view is the first one, and only one who wants the fledglings or the eggs has a mitzva to send away the mother and take them. But one who is not interested in them has no mitzva to send away the mother and take them, and consequently one should not do so, because of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim and bal tashḥit. And if he wishes to fulfill the mitzva according to the second view, it is better that he chase the mother off the nest with a shout or a light tap on the nest, and not take the fledglings or the eggs. For some say that by chasing the mother off the nest, so that according to halakha he is able to take the fledglings or the eggs, he already fulfills the mitzva, and in this way he fulfills the mitzva without clashing with the position of the first view (Responsa Ḥakham Tzvi 83; Shevet Yehuda YD 292; Or Same'aḥ, Hilkhot Yom Tov 3:8).4

sections.title: Details of the Laws
sections.html:
The mitzva of shilu'aḥ ha-ken applies only to species of kosher birds. Therefore one must know how to distinguish between the species that are kosher for eating and the non-kosher ones. The kosher species found in our surroundings are: pigeons, turtledoves and the house sparrow.

Likewise, one must distinguish between the male and the female, for the mitzva of shilu'aḥ ha-ken applies only when the mother is sitting on her chicks. In practice, with pigeons and turtledoves, during most hours of the day the male sits, and the mother sits from about five in the evening until seven in the morning; if he sends her away, he fulfills the mitzva. But if he comes in the middle of the day, he will likely find the male, and if he sends it away and takes the fledglings, he does not fulfill a mitzva. However, the male sparrow sits on the nest only about two hours a day, and its identifying sign is that it has a black patch on its chest.

One must also know that if the nest was built within his guarded yard or on his roof, the moment the mother flies off her nest, his yard acquires the eggs and the chicks for him, and he has no mitzva to send away the mother. Only if he stipulates in his mind, when the birds begin to build the nest, that he does not want the nest to belong to him, will he have a mitzva in sending away the mother.5

According to most poskim, sending away the mother can be done by chasing her from the nest with a shout or by striking the nest with one's hand or a stick. According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Sheḥita 13:5), only if he grasps the mother by her wings and sends her off does he fulfill the mitzva. On the other hand, however, there is a concern that perhaps according to several Rishonim, if he grasps the mother by her wings he transgresses a prohibition, which he indeed rectifies after he sends her away, but in the meantime, while he is holding her, he has a prohibition in his hands. Therefore it is proper to send away the mother with a shout or a blow.6
